title: German Africa
capsule: German colonial Africa comprised four principal territories acquired after 1884: German East Africa (modern Tanzania, Rwanda, and Burundi), German South West Africa (Namibia), Kamerun (Cameroon and part of modern Central African Republic), and Togoland. Formal German colonial expansion began with the Berlin Conference of 1884–85, and within a decade Germany had consolidated control through treaties, often extracted by coercion, and military campaigns. The most notorious episode was the Herero and Nama genocide (1904–1908) in German South West Africa, in which General Lothar von Trotha issued an extermination order that killed an estimated 65,000–80,000 Herero and 10,000 Nama. All German colonies were stripped from Germany by the Treaty of Versailles (1919) and redistributed as League of Nations mandates to Britain, France, Belgium, Portugal, and South Africa.
attestation: Boundaries from Seshat Cliopatria (Bennett et al., Scientific Data 2025; CC BY 4.0), digitized from standard historical atlases at ~0.07° resolution. Colonial boundaries of German Africa are defined by the Berlin Conference protocols, subsequent bilateral treaties, and documented in detailed colonial cartography; boundaries are well attested for the post-1884 period, though pre-1890 peripheral zones varied as treaties were renegotiated.
